title: The Giant Magnet Under Your Feet

pages.text: Rub a sewing needle along a magnet about thirty times, always in the same direction. Rest the needle on a small piece of leaf floating in a bowl of water. The leaf turns slowly, then stops. Push it round and it swings back to the same line: one end pointing north, the other south. You have made a compass. Whether you try this in Axim, Accra, or Bolgatanga, the needle lines up the same way. Something is pulling on it that no one can see. That something is Earth’s magnetic field, and it comes from deep beneath your feet.

That something is Earth’s magnetic field, and it comes from deep beneath your feet.
pages.alt: A sewing needle resting on a small green leaf floating in a bowl of water, with an arrow showing north.

pages.text: Earth behaves like a giant magnet. About 2,900 kilometres below the surface lies the outer core, a layer of liquid iron and nickel hotter than 4,000 °C. As the planet spins, this liquid metal flows, and the moving metal produces a magnetic field that reaches far out into space. A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where its force can be felt. Earth’s field does more than guide a compass. It turns aside most of the harmful particles that stream from the Sun. Sea turtles, like those that nest on the beaches near Ada, can sense the field and use it to find their way.

pages.text: Now look at a map of the Atlantic Ocean. The coast of West Africa, from Ghana round to Nigeria and Cameroon, looks as if it would fit neatly against the bulge of Brazil, like two pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. In 1912, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener said this was no accident. He pointed out that matching rocks, and fossils of the same ancient animals, are found on both sides of the ocean. He proposed that the continents were once joined in one huge landmass, later named Pangaea, and had slowly drifted apart. Most scientists laughed. How could a continent move?
sentences: Now look at a map of the Atlantic Ocean.
The coast of West Africa, from Ghana round to Nigeria and Cameroon, looks as if it would fit neatly against the bulge of Brazil, like two pieces of a jigsaw puzzle.
In 1912, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener said this was no accident.
He pointed out that matching rocks, and fossils of the same ancient animals, are found on both sides of the ocean.
He proposed that the continents were once joined in one huge landmass, later named Pangaea, and had slowly drifted apart.
Most scientists laughed.
How could a continent move?
pages.alt: A map of the Atlantic with Africa and South America drawn close together so that the coast of West Africa fits against Brazil.

pages.text: The answer came from the sea floor in the 1950s and 1960s. Earth’s outer shell is broken into huge slabs called tectonic plates, which move a few centimetres each year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Down the middle of the Atlantic runs a long chain of undersea mountains. There, two plates pull apart and hot liquid rock, called magma, rises to fill the gap. It cools into new sea floor. So the ocean grows wider, and Africa and South America, which began to separate about 130 million years ago, move a little further apart every year.
sentences: The answer came from the sea floor in the 1950s and 1960s.

Down the middle of the Atlantic runs a long chain of undersea mountains.
There, two plates pull apart and hot liquid rock, called magma, rises to fill the gap.
It cools into new sea floor.
So the ocean grows wider, and Africa and South America, which began to separate about 130 million years ago, move a little further apart every year.
pages.alt: A cross-section of the sea floor showing two plates moving apart at an undersea ridge, with magma rising between them.

pages.text: Here the two stories meet. Magma contains tiny grains of iron-rich minerals. While the rock is liquid, the grains turn to line up with Earth’s magnetic field, like millions of compass needles. When the rock hardens, they are locked in place. Ships towing instruments across the Atlantic found something strange: stripes of rock magnetised towards the north, next to stripes magnetised towards the south. The pattern was the same on both sides of the ridge. It showed that new sea floor keeps spreading outwards, and that Earth’s field has swapped direction many times. Each swap is called a magnetic reversal.

pages.alt: Bands of sea-floor rock in two alternating colours, arranged as a mirror image on each side of an undersea ridge.

pages.text: The last full reversal happened about 780,000 years ago. Since the 1800s, the field has weakened by roughly a tenth, and some reports claim that a flip is about to happen. Most scientists disagree. The field has grown weaker and stronger many times without reversing, a reversal takes thousands of years, and no past reversal has been linked to a disaster for living things. Moving plates matter more to daily life. Ghana lies far from a plate edge, yet old cracks in the rock near Accra still slip. In 1939, an earthquake there killed 17 people. The ground beneath us is never completely still.

activities.question: What produces Earth’s magnetic field?
options: A giant bar of solid iron buried at the North Pole
Liquid iron and nickel flowing in the outer core
Magnetic rocks lying on the sea floor

activities.question: Which evidence did Wegener use to argue that the continents were once joined?
options: Matching rocks and fossils on both sides of the Atlantic
Stripes of magnetised rock on the sea floor

activities.question: What do the magnetic stripes on the floor of the Atlantic show?
options: That a compass does not work at sea
New sea floor spreads from the ridge and Earth’s field has reversed many times

activities.question: Apply it: A website claims that Earth’s magnetic field will flip next year and wipe out life. Using the article, what is the best reply?
options: It is true, because the field has weakened
Reversals take thousands of years and are not linked to disasters for life
It cannot be true, because the field has never reversed

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: Africa and South America begin to separate
The last full magnetic reversal takes place
Wegener proposes that the continents drift
Ships map magnetic stripes on the Atlantic floor

activities.definition: A huge slab of Earth’s outer shell that moves very slowly.
distractors: A flat stone used for grinding pepper
A layer of liquid metal in Earth’s core

glossary.definition: Magnetic field: the region around a magnet where its force can be felt.
An instrument with a magnetised needle that lines up north to south.
Outer core: the layer of liquid iron and nickel deep inside Earth.
Tectonic plate: a huge slab of Earth’s outer shell that moves very slowly.
Hot liquid rock from inside Earth.
Magnetic reversal: a change in which Earth’s magnetic north and south swap places.
